question: In Ayorinde v. Team Industrial Services, what framework and prima facie elements does the Fifth Circuit apply to a Title VII retaliation claim that rests on circumstantial evidence?
reference_notes: Must mention: the McDonnell Douglas framework applies; the plaintiff must show protected activity, an adverse employment action, and a causal connection between them.
cited_authority: Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53, 56 (2006)
rater_a_reason: cl10737190:5 states the circumstantial-evidence McDonnell Douglas rule and the three prima facie elements.

question: Why did the Fifth Circuit in Ayorinde v. Team Industrial Services hold that Ayorinde failed to exhaust his constructive discharge claim?
reference_notes: Must mention: neither EEOC charge contained allegations like or related to constructive discharge; the resignation letter has no bearing on exhaustion; the charges made no reference to his resignation or to intolerable conditions.
cited_authority: Aryain v. Wal-Mart Stores Texas LP, 534 F.3d 473, 480 (5th Cir. 2008)
rater_a_reason: cl10737190:7 explains the charges lacked related allegations and that the resignation letter is irrelevant.

question: According to the Seventh Circuit in Paterakos v. City of Chicago, what must an employee show to prove FMLA retaliation, and how can an employer defeat FMLA liability when it disciplines an employee over suspected leave abuse?
reference_notes: Must mention: retaliation requires FMLA-protected activity, an adverse employment action and a causal connection; an employer may defeat liability by showing an honest suspicion that the employee was abusing leave.
cited_authority: Juday v. FCA US LLC, 57 F.4th 591, 595 (7th Cir. 2023)
rater_a_reason: cl11118835:17 lists the retaliation elements and states the honest-suspicion defense.

question: Why did the Seventh Circuit in Paterakos v. City of Chicago conclude that a one-week assignment to a second call center was not an adverse employment action even under the Muldrow standard?
reference_notes: Must mention: Muldrow does not require significant harm but the plaintiff must show some harm; the assignment did not reduce responsibilities, pay or benefits; the half-hour shift change and new location were minor and caused no objective harm.
cited_authority: Ellis v. CCA of Tennessee LLC, 650 F.3d 640, 650 (7th Cir. 2011)
rater_a_reason: cl11118835:11 holds no harm was shown, cites the unchanged pay and duties, and treats the minor shift and location changes as insufficient.

question: Why did the Fifth Circuit in Rodriguez v. City of Corpus Christi reject Rodriguez's Title VII and Equal Pay Act pay-discrimination claims at summary judgment?
reference_notes: Must mention: both claims required a proper comparator who was paid more for substantially the same work; Rodriguez named only Gonzalez, and the City never paid her less than Gonzalez.
cited_authority: Taylor v. United Parcel Serv., Inc., 554 F.3d 510, 522 (5th Cir. 2008)
rater_a_reason: cl10815384:9 states the comparator requirement for Title VII/EPA and that Gonzalez, the only named comparator, was never paid more than Rodriguez.

cited_authority: Aryain v. Wal-Mart Stores Texas LP, 534 F.3d 473, 480 (5th Cir. 2008)

claim: Under Fifth Circuit law, an FLSA retaliation plaintiff must show protected activity, an adverse action and a causal link, and an informal complaint counts as protected activity only if it is clear and detailed enough for a reasonable employer to see it as an assertion of statutory rights.
label: supported
cited_authority: Kasten v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics Corp., 563 U.S. 1, 14 (2011)
rater_a_reason: Step 1: cl10815384:7 states the three FLSA retaliation elements and the 'sufficiently clear and detailed' complaint standard.
construction_note: Faithful paraphrase of the FLSA retaliation elements and Kasten-based complaint standard in the cited chunk. Same-opinion distractor cl10815384:6 (sham affidavit); other-opinion chunks concern Title VII/FMLA retaliation elements, not FLSA.

claim: The Fifth Circuit concluded that the City's voluntary payment of overtime to Rodriguez for a limited time did not destroy her exempt status, because she still received a guaranteed amount on a salary basis.
label: right_doc_wrong_passage
cited_authority: Helix Energy Sols. Grp., Inc. v. Hewitt, 598 U.S. 39, 43 (2023)
rater_a_reason: Step 2: the conclusion that voluntary overtime did not destroy exempt status is in cl10815384:13 ('This additional compensation did not destroy Rodriguez's exempt status'); cited cl10815384:12 states only the legal rule and pay record.
construction_note: Claim paraphrases the conclusion in cl10815384:13; cited the preceding Rodriguez chunk, which sets out the salary-basis rule and paystub facts but not the overtime-does-not-destroy-exemption conclusion.

claim: In the Seventh Circuit, a plaintiff can show pretext without proving the employer's stated reason is factually untrue, since a true fact may not be the honest reason; pretext may be shown by an explanation with no basis in fact, ambiguous or suggestive conduct, or better treatment of similarly situated employees.
label: supported
cited_authority: Vichio v. US Foods, Inc., 88 F.4th 687, 691 (7th Cir. 2023)
rater_a_reason: Step 1: cl11118835:12 says a true fact can still be a pretext and lists the three ways of proving pretext.
construction_note: Faithful paraphrase of the pretext paragraph in the cited chunk. Other-opinion chunks address McDonnell Douglas burden shifting and Fifth Circuit pretext but not these points.

claim: The sham affidavit doctrine lets a court disregard an affidavit only when it is so markedly inconsistent with earlier testimony as to be an obvious sham; the bar is high, and an affidavit that merely supplements prior testimony is not a sham.
label: wrong_document
cited_authority: Stalter v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 195 F.3d 285, 290–91 (7th Cir. 1999)
rater_a_reason: Step 3: the sham-affidavit standard is stated in cl10815384:6 (Rodriguez, a different opinion); cl11118835:15 and the other Paterakos chunk do not discuss it.
construction_note: Claim paraphrases the sham affidavit passage in cl10815384:6; cited a Paterakos pretext chunk on a nearby summary-judgment theme that does not mention the doctrine.
